Taiwan-based market intelligence firm TrendForce says Chinese cloud service providers are grappling with GPU shortages, high inventories, and fierce competition over AI token pricing.

But don't get too excited: TrendForce forecasts overall NAND flash contract prices falling by 0-5 percent quarter on quarter in early 2027, with all product categories entering a downturn from the second quarter.

Falling orders are only half the story. Manufacturers are also increasing output, while weaker consumer electronics sales could further depress demand.

Strong demand for high-performance storage in the US continues to drive manufacturers to expand capacity and upgrade to newer process technologies. items.title: Mouse fight club might explain why we like to watch violent things

Credit: J.M. Iravedra-Garcia et al., 2026

There's something about watching violent events that broadly appeals to us, whether it's the latest John Wick movie, a video game, or a live UFC bout. Scientists have debated whether watching violent things could make us more aggressive, but it could also be an adaptive survival strategy. Male mice, for instance, who watch other mice fighting learned enough about how to fight to better protect themselves (compared to mice who didn't watch fights) when pitted against stronger, more aggressive opponents, according to a paper published in the journal Nature.

The team assigned male mice randomly to three different groups—fighters, spectators, or novices—and then subjected each group to eight days of training involving three 10-minute sessions per day. The novices played with stuffed mice in isolation, while the spectators watched various pairs of fighter mice battle it out from a raised platform behind a transparent barrier—a set-up chosen to let them smell and listen to the fights as well as observe them.

items.title: Voyager 1 celebrates one light-day with a nice lie-down
items.summary:
Voyager 1 marked its milestone of one light-day from Earth in time-honored fashion: by giving controllers the silent treatment.

On November 14, the mission team noticed that the veteran spacecraft had stopped returning science and engineering data. A Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra, Australia, picked up its carrier signal, but no data.

The carrier signal indicates that Voyager 1 can still keep its antenna pointed at Earth and operate its transmitting equipment. However, something could be amiss with the system responsible for collecting and collating data from the spacecraft.

Something similar happened in 2023 . After a few months of troubleshooting, engineers managed to coax a response from the probe, and by June 2024, NASA was delighted to announce that the spacecraft was back in action.

The problem was traced to a faulty computer chip, and engineers devised a software update to work around the defective hardware. That experience will stand the team in good stead this time around.

There was also a brief interruption in communications with Voyager 1 in October, which could have been caused by the spacecraft dropping into safe mode after a thruster failover occurred. Engineers are investigating whether the two incidents are connected.

The Voyagers have an impressive amount of fault protection built in, which has contributed to their extraordinary longevity. It will be half a century in 2027 since the spacecraft were launched, so glitches are understandable and likely.

NASA expects to confirm on November 19 that Voyager 1 was still operating when it reached…

“At this time, we have found no evidence of active exploitation of any of these vulnerabilities in the wild,” and F5 spokesperson told The Register . “We continue to monitor closely and will share updates via myF5 as we learn more.”

As with all of the other recently disclosed vulnerabilities in foundational technologies like PHP, Apache, and Java, these critical NGINX bugs were uncovered by researchers using AI. One of them has been hiding in the code for at least 10 years.

Tomer Schwartz, Wiz’s chief technology officer of exposure management and AppSec, helped find the bug, along with researchers from Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint working independently. 

Schwartz told The Register that this wave of AI-discovered flaws “point to a new reality.”

“We need to treat every internet-connected system as potentially vulnerable,” Schwartz said. “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how quickly longstanding risks can become real threats.” 

NGINX is the world’s most widely used open source web server, handling HTTPS requests and routing incoming traffic to the right application or API. It powers about a third of all websites (around 225 million ),…
items.t: AI found more critical bugs in another widely used technology running 225M websites

items.title: To rank the world's biggest supercomputers, we're gonna need a bigger bench
items.summary:
For decades, the Top500 list has tirelessly ranked the world’s biggest, most powerful, and often most unique publicly-known supercomputers.

With the rise of generative AI, the list no longer lives up to its name. China’s Lineshine supercomputer at 2.2 exaFLOPS of double precision compute in the High-Performance Linpack (HPL) benchmark may be the top system on the bi-annual ranking, but it’s nowhere near the biggest compute cluster in the world.

Superclusters like SpaceXAI’s Colossus, Meta’s Promethius, and OpenAI’s Stargate pack hundreds of thousands of GPUs, dwarfing anything on the Top500 today.

“These [companies] are not interested in submitting to the Top500,” Eth Zürich’s Torsten Hoefler said during his Supercomputing address this week.

It’s a dilemma that the founders of the Top500 ranking are now grappling with. And some believe it may be time for a rethink.

“What’s really needed for tracking that more appropriately is not just a different benchmark but also different methodology,” Top500 author Erich Strohmaier said.

For a long time, Strohmaier explains, compute capability was roughly aligned with capacity.

What happened in the last few years with AI is “capacity really pulled ahead of capability in terms of market size,” he said. “We were and we still are very focused on capability.”

By capability, Strohmaier is referring to the ability to run one code across the entire cluster.

“Our prime rule for benchmarking is, you have to benchmark your whole system with one code and you cannot just add two parts up to make up a number,” he explained.

items.title: The "shameful" measles data that lost the US its elimination status
items.summary:
International health authorities formally announced on Tuesday that the US has lost its measles elimination status, a hard-fought public health triumph won in 2000 after decades-long vaccination efforts. The loss had been widely expected by public health experts for months, and the decision was leaked by the press last week. Still, having the designation officially stripped stings.

After the announcement Tuesday, public health experts, doctors, and political leaders decried the dramatic backslide for the US, calling it " shameful " and a " national embarrassment ." News articles point to the staggering vertical rise of measles cases this year, currently over 5,400 cases , more than any other year since 1991. An explosive measles outbreak in Pennsylvania accounts for over 1,500 of those cases . There have been 10 confirmed deaths across three states, several deaths just in the last week.

But the measles data that caused the US to lose its status—the bits of it that are public at least—paint a darker picture of where the US is in its rematch with measles, the most contagious virus known on Earth. For one thing, almost none of the data from this year—the cases, the explosive Pennsylvania outbreak, the deaths—factored in to the loss. It was lost earlier. What's happening now is a runaway epidemic.

items.title: Cyber insurers now want proof you can actually recover
items.summary:
Cyber insurance pricing has cooled. Marsh’s Global Insurance Market Index shows global cyber rates falling for a 13th consecutive quarter, with US rates recently stabilizing after the ransomware-driven spikes of 2020 and 2021 . 

Part of the reason rates are lowering is because carriers are imposing stricter requirements that determine if you will qualify at all. A major global carrier recently stopped writing law firms altogether because of claims volume, and brokers expect healthcare and managed service providers (MSPs) to be next.

The newest requirement is the one many MSPs are least ready for: proof that you can actually recover. This is what insurers really want to see, and meeting the bar is harder than it sounds.

Why insurers stopped taking backups on faith In a recent webinar with cyber insurance provider Beltex , the familiar list of requirements came up first:

Multifactor authentication (MFA) on external access and privileged accounts

Endpoint detection and response (EDR) on every endpoint

A staffed 24/7 team where managed detection and response (MDR) is required, and timely patching.

Backup is now joining that list, and for good reason. For years it was assumed that having backups and a green job status was good enough. Claims have shown otherwise.

Now, attackers go after backup infrastructure to make their ransomware more effective, and an untested restore can re-infect the production network.
